loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 5 of 6 · Storage integration — the VolumeSnapshotClass example
orig:
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1beta1
driver: hostpath.csi.k8s.io
kind: VolumeSnapshotClass
metadata:
  annotations:
    k10.kasten.io/is-snapshot-class: "true"
  name: csi-hostpath-snapclass

The documented Beta CSI Snapshot API example. The driver and name values belong to the sample hostpath driver — yours will differ [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.103].
prop:
apiVersion: snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1
driver: hostpath.csi.k8s.io
kind: VolumeSnapshotClass
metadata:
  annotations:
    k10.kasten.io/is-snapshot-class: "true"
  name: csi-hostpath-snapclass

The annotation is what matters; the API group has moved on. The guide illustrates this object with its Alpha and Beta snapshot API examples [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102, p.103], but on every Kubernetes release Veeam Kasten 9.0.2 supports — 1.29 and later [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862] — the group is snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1, as in the guide's own Azure VolumeSnapshotClass [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.105]. The driver and name values belong to the sample hostpath driver — yours will differ.
why: The module hands a platform team a manifest that cannot be applied to any cluster this release supports. snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1beta1 was removed from Kubernetes in 1.21; the supported matrix starts at Kubernetes 1.29 (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862). A learner who copies this block gets 'no matches for kind VolumeSnapshotClass in version snapshot.storage.k8s.io/v1beta1' and, in the middle of a deployment, will reasonably suspect their cluster rather than the manifest. The guide itself shows a working v1 VolumeSnapshotClass carrying the same Veeam Kasten annotation (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.105). The upstream doc keeping a beta example is upstream's problem; reproducing it as the copy-paste artifact in a course is ours.

loc: Lesson02_Kubernetes_Foundations_for_Backup_Admins.html · Section 06 · caption under the VolumeSnapshotClass code block
orig: K10 appears inside the annotation key because that is the product's technical namespace in the API; the product name is Veeam Kasten.
prop: k10 appears in lowercase inside the annotation key k10.kasten.io/is-snapshot-class because that key is a verbatim technical string; the product name is Veeam Kasten for Kubernetes.
why: Two problems in one sentence. (1) Naming standard and glossary.md "K10" note: "K10" is permitted only inside verbatim technical strings — but the string in the code block directly above is lowercase (k10.kasten.io/is-snapshot-class), so the caption's uppercase "K10" is not the verbatim string it claims to be and reintroduces the retired product name as prose. (2) "the product's technical namespace in the API" is imprecise — k10.kasten.io is the annotation key's domain prefix, not a Kubernetes namespace, and the module has just spent a section teaching the learner what a namespace is. Same paragraph also carries the only remaining uppercase K10 in the six files, so fixing it clears the naming check course-wide.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 1 of 6 · Prerequisites — The three CSI requirements
orig:
The three CSI requirements

  • Kubernetes v1.14.0 or higher [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102].
  • The VolumeSnapshotDataSource feature has been enabled in the Kubernetes cluster [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102].
  • A CSI driver that has Volume Snapshot support [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102].
prop:
The three CSI requirements

  • Kubernetes v1.14.0 or higher [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102].
  • The VolumeSnapshotDataSource feature has been enabled in the Kubernetes cluster [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102].
  • A CSI driver that has Volume Snapshot support [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102].

Read the first two against the release you are actually running. The Storage Integration page states the baseline as Kubernetes v1.14.0 with the VolumeSnapshotDataSource feature enabled [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102], while the versions Veeam Kasten 9.0.2 supports begin at Kubernetes 1.29 [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862] — far past the point where volume snapshots became a stable API, so there is no feature gate left for you to switch on. The third requirement is the one that still has to be proved on your cluster, and Section 2 is how you prove it.
why: Accurate quotation, misleading as a checklist. The v1.14.0 floor and the VolumeSnapshotDataSource feature gate are the guide's own words (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102), but they describe a Kubernetes generation this release no longer supports: the certified matrix runs 1.29 to 1.34 (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.862), and the gate no longer exists on any of them. An admin sent to verify a feature gate that cannot be found either wastes an afternoon or concludes the prerequisite is unmet and stalls the install. Keeping the quotation and adding the version context costs three sentences and removes both failure modes.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 2 of 6 · Pre-flight checks — deployment-readiness checklist, blocking item 5
why: The checklist gates the install on the cheap check and leaves the only real proof of the snapshot path as a Pro tip. The basic primer run validates settings, catalogs StorageClasses and does basic CSI validation (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.7); it is the CSI invocation — 'curl … | bash /dev/stdin csi -s ${STORAGE_CLASS}' — that writes data, snapshots it, provisions a new volume from the snapshot and validates the data (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102). In engagements, the drivers that pass the basic check and fail the round trip are exactly the ones that ruin a first backup window. If a checklist has five blocking items, the snapshot round trip belongs among them.

loc: Lesson05_Restores_and_Day_to_Day_Administration.html · Who can do what · 04 — bind the administrator role
orig: That is the command form for an individual user or service account [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.266]. You will do it from the dashboard most of the time, which is the next part.
prop: That is the command form for an individual user or service account [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.266], and on its own it is not the whole grant. In addition to the k10-admin ClusterRole, administrators also require the k10-ns-admin Role for Secret and ConfigMap access within the Veeam Kasten install namespace [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.267]; that Role needs a RoleBinding in the release namespace, and Veeam Kasten creates one for the default group k10:admins, so adding the user to that group covers both bindings at once [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.268]. You will do it from the dashboard most of the time, which is the next part.
why: A team following this section literally ends up with a half-privileged administrator. The guide is explicit: 'In addition to the k10-admin ClusterRole, administrators also require the k10-ns-admin Role for Secret and ConfigMap access within the Veeam Kasten install namespace' (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.267), bound by a RoleBinding in the release namespace, with a RoleBinding for the k10:admins group created for you (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.268). The symptom in the field is an 'administrator' who can drive the dashboard until an operation touches a Secret — creating a location profile credential, for instance — and then fails on permissions. The module names four roles and omits the one that makes the first of them work.

loc: Lesson05_Restores_and_Day_to_Day_Administration.html · Restores · 02 — Applications, and the virtual machines among them
orig: Do not let the familiarity carry you too far, though. Virtual machines can only be restored into a new namespace [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.417]. The in-place restore you would reach for out of habit is not on the menu for that object type.
prop: Do not let the familiarity carry you too far, though. In the guide's discussion of renaming a restored application's persistent volume claims — which for a virtual machine also means renaming its DataVolumes and transforming the references and owner references to them — it states that VirtualMachines can only be restored into a new namespace [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.417]. The virtual-machine restore workflow itself is documented as similar to restoring any other application, initiated from the Restore Points page against the Virtual Machine application type [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.544, p.545]. Prove which target namespaces your platform actually accepts with a test restore before a runbook depends on the answer.
why: The sentence is real but its scope is not. 'VirtualMachines can only be restored into a new namespace' sits at the end of the PVC-renaming and transform discussion on Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.417, in a paragraph about renaming a VM's PVCs and DataVolumes; the virtual-machine restore section itself describes the workflow as similar to any other application with no such restriction (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.544, p.545). Lifted out and stated flatly — 'the in-place restore … is not on the menu' — it tells an OpenShift Virtualization team their in-place VM recovery path does not exist, which changes how they write their DR plan. Scope it to what the page says and route the rest to a test.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 6 of 6 · Your first location profile — Pointing it at a Veeam repository
orig:
Four things to know before you choose this route

  • Exporting to a Veeam Repository requires the use of the Block Mode Export mechanism for all volume snapshots created by the policy, and when a Veeam Repository is selected as the Export Location Profile, block mode export is enabled automatically [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.128].
  • Veeam Kasten does not support export to Veeam Backup & Replication direct object storage repository types [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.128].
  • Each Veeam Kasten instance may only export to a single, unique Veeam Backup & Replication backup server; multiple location profiles may be created to export to separate repositories exposed by the same backup server, and multiple Veeam Kasten instances may be integrated with the same backup server [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129].
  • In order to properly restore volume data, the name of the Veeam Repository location profile on both the source and target cluster must be identical [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.130].
prop:
Five things to know before you choose this route

  • Exporting to a Veeam Repository requires the use of the Block Mode Export mechanism for all volume snapshots created by the policy, and when a Veeam Repository is selected as the Export Location Profile, block mode export is enabled automatically [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.128].
  • Veeam Kasten does not support export to Veeam Backup & Replication direct object storage repository types [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.128].
  • Each Veeam Kasten instance may only export to a single, unique Veeam Backup & Replication backup server; multiple location profiles may be created to export to separate repositories exposed by the same backup server, and multiple Veeam Kasten instances may be integrated with the same backup server [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129].
  • In order to properly restore volume data, the name of the Veeam Repository location profile on both the source and target cluster must be identical [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.130].
  • Your CSI driver decides how expensive each export is. Veeam Kasten accelerates incremental backups to Veeam Backup & Replication for Azure Disk CSI (disk.csi.azure.com), CephRBD CSI (rbd.csi.ceph.com) and VMware vSphere CSI (csi.vsphere.vmware.com); where that storage integration is unavailable, each export reads the entire source volume, and only the changes are sent to Veeam Backup & Replication [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129].
why: This is the sizing fact the route lives or dies on, and it is missing. Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.129 lists the three provisioners with integrations that accelerate incremental backups to Veeam Backup & Replication and states that without them 'each export will require reading the entire source volume(s), however only changes will be sent to VBR'. A Veeam Data Platform administrator reading this section will price the export window from their familiar incremental-forever mental model and be wrong by the size of the volume on every run. It is also the fact that decides whether a nightly export against multi-terabyte claims fits in the window at all.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 4 of 6 · Dashboard and authentication — The four authentication modes
orig:
The four authentication modes

During installation, you have an option to choose an authentication mode: Direct Access, Basic Authentication, Token-based Authentication, or OpenID Connect [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.208]. When exposing the Veeam Kasten dashboard externally, it is required that an authentication method is properly configured to secure access [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.220].
prop:
The four authentication modes you choose at install

During installation, you have an option to choose an authentication mode: Direct Access, Basic Authentication, Token-based Authentication, or OpenID Connect [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.208]. When exposing the Veeam Kasten dashboard externally, it is required that an authentication method is properly configured to secure access [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.220]. Two more modes exist beyond that install-time list, and both matter in an enterprise: access can be authenticated against an Active Directory or LDAP server, enabled with --set auth.ldap.enabled=true and its supporting Helm values [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.250], and on Red Hat OpenShift the OpenShift OAuth server can do the authenticating, enabled with --set auth.openshift.enabled=true [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.237].
why: The four modes on Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.208 are the install-time picker, not the feature surface, and the omission has a predictable consequence: the first question a Veeam Data Platform administrator asks about any console is whether it can use Active Directory. It can — the guide documents an Active Directory/LDAP mode with its own Helm values (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.250) and an OpenShift OAuth mode (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.237), which this module already half-mentions in the OpenShift Route tab. Leaving AD/LDAP out of a section headed 'The four authentication modes' reads as a statement that it is not supported.

prop: the deployment and release information available from Helm v3 — Helm is Kubernetes' package manager, covered fully in Module 02, so file the term away rather than chasing it now — and all of the persistent storage resources associated with those workloads, meaning the PersistentVolumeClaims and PersistentVolumes [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.346].

In a live read-aloud this is exactly where a backup admin interrupts with 'wait, what's Helm?' and the presenter has nothing to say except 'hang on, Module 02.' The course already handles this well elsewhere (the hero prereqs box promises every term is 'defined on the spot or deferred to Module 02') — this is the one spot in the opening minutes where that promise isn't kept inline. loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 6 of 6 · Your first location profile
orig: If the bucket has object locking enabled, set the Enable Immutable Backups toggle [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315].
prop: If the bucket has object locking enabled, set the Enable Immutable Backups toggle — this is the setting that keeps a restore point from being deleted or overwritten by anyone or anything, including ransomware operating with valid credentials, until its retention expires [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315].
why: Immutability and ransomware resilience is one of the three value stories this course is supposed to land, and this is the only place in the whole course where the general-purpose immutability toggle for ordinary application backups is introduced — and it's introduced as a bare checkbox with a bucket-setting prerequisite, nothing else. A VDP admin audience cares about this specific checkbox more than almost anything else on the page; it's the line I'd want to slow down on in a demo, and as written there's nothing to slow down for. (Immutability does get a strong ransomware framing later, in Lesson 04's KDR section — but that's a module away and about protecting Kasten's own catalog, not this general location-profile setting. The benefit shouldn't wait that long.)

prop: Veeam Kasten also supports a more flexible permissions model that scopes a user's permissions to perform actions only within the context of specified applications [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.263] — the middle ground between k10-admin's everything and k10-basic's whole namespace, for the case where one team owns several applications inside a namespace they don't otherwise control.
why: This sentence lands right after the four built-in roles have been cleanly explained, table and all — the section is doing well up to this point — and then names a fifth capability, calls it 'more flexible,' and moves on without saying what it actually does or when you'd reach for it instead of the roles just covered. That's the exact shape of a demo stall: a platform team or a VDP admin who just followed the k10-admin / k10-basic / k10-config-view logic hears 'also supports a more flexible model' and asks 'flexible how?' — and the page has already turned the page on them. loc: Lesson02_Kubernetes_Foundations_for_Backup_Admins.html · section#kasten ("Where Veeam Kasten sits in all of this")
orig: Because it runs as pods among other pods, its security posture is a cluster concern: all Veeam Kasten pods enable a read-only root filesystem security context by default, with writable paths backed by dedicated volume mounts [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1096].
prop: Because it runs as pods among other pods, its security posture is a cluster concern: all Veeam Kasten pods enable a read-only root filesystem security context by default, with writable paths backed by dedicated volume mounts [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1096]. On Red Hat OpenShift specifically, this is also a Security Context Constraint (SCC) question — which SCC the Veeam Kasten pods run under, and whether the cluster's default restricted-v2 SCC is sufficient or a custom SCC is required, is not addressed here [VERIFY: confirm Veeam Kasten's SCC requirements on OpenShift against the installation reference before an architect relies on this section].
why: This course discusses OpenShift extensively (Routes, DeploymentConfig, OAuth proxy, OKD, Red Hat OpenShift Virtualization) and this exact passage is making a hardening/security-posture claim, but Security Context Constraints — the single most common day-one blocker when running third-party Helm charts on OpenShift, and the first thing an OpenShift architect checks before an install — are never mentioned anywhere in the course. An expert reader hits 'its security posture is a cluster concern' and immediately asks 'under which SCC' — leaving that unanswered on an OpenShift-heavy course costs credibility. Flagged as an expertise-based doubt for SME confirmation, not asserted as fact, per the persona's hard rules.

loc: Lesson04_Maintaining_Veeam_Kasten_Over_Time.html · Protecting the catalog · 04 — the Veeam Data Platform parallel
orig: The Veeam Data Platform parallel is configuration backup, and it holds up well: both protect the metadata that makes restore points findable, both are scheduled, and both are worthless if you cannot decrypt them. Where it breaks is the dependency list. A KDR recovery needs three things you must arrange in advance — a location profile that the target cluster can also reach, the passphrase used when KDR was configured, and the source instance's cluster identifier [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.571].
prop: The Veeam Data Platform parallel is configuration backup, and it holds up well: both protect the metadata that makes restore points findable, both are scheduled, and both are worthless if you cannot decrypt them. Where it breaks is the dependency list. The guide is blunt about what to retain after enabling KDR, without which restore point catalog recovery will not be possible: the source Cluster ID, the KDR passphrase or the external secret manager details, and the KDR location profile details and credential [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.585].
why: Right facts, wrong page. Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.571 covers enabling KDR and the immutable-profile recommendation; the three-item retention warning — 'The source Cluster ID / The KDR passphrase (or external secret manager details) / The KDR location profile details and credential … Without this information, restore point catalog recovery will not be possible' — is on p.585. This is the one row in the module a reader will follow the citation on, because it is the list they have to hand to whoever holds the secrets store, and the guide's own wording is stronger than the paraphrase.

loc: Lesson04_Maintaining_Veeam_Kasten_Over_Time.html · Upgrades · 02 — the two rules that decide your upgrade plan
orig: You do not have to work the arithmetic out by hand. You can verify available catalog free space and see your recommended upgrade path from the System Information page under the Settings menu in the navigation sidebar [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.198]. The k10tools binary offers the same answer from a terminal: its k10tools primer upgrade sub-command finds the recommended upgrade path for your version and checks there is adequate space, for Helm deployments [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.872].
prop: You do not have to work the arithmetic out by hand. You can verify available catalog free space and see your recommended upgrade path from the System Information page under the Settings menu in the navigation sidebar [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.198]. The k10tools binary offers the same answer from a terminal: its k10tools primer upgrade sub-command finds the recommended upgrade path for your version and checks there is adequate space, for Helm deployments — and it requires internet access to gcr.io, so on a restricted or air-gapped cluster the System Information page is the route that still works [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.872].
why: One clause from the same page, and it is the one that decides which of the two routes a regulated estate can use. Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.872 states of the upgrade primer: 'This tool requires Internet access to http://gcr.io'. Air-gapped and egress-restricted clusters are common in the estates this course is aimed at — the module already teaches the air-gapped primer variant in Module 03 — so an admin who reaches for the terminal answer on such a cluster gets a failure with no hint that the dashboard route is unaffected.

loc: Lesson02_Kubernetes_Foundations_for_Backup_Admins.html · Concept · 06 — VolumeSnapshots, and why drivers differ (Where it is sharper here, item 03)

prop:
Snapshot plus export is the shape of a real policy.
Snapshots give you speed on the cluster; an exported backup gives you the copy that survives the cluster. You need both, and that is a policy decision you will make in Module 05.
why: Wrong forward pointer. Policies — snapshot frequency, Enable Backups via Snapshot Exports, retention — are built in Module 05, Section 01; Module 04 is upgrades, monitoring, KDR and housekeeping. A learner who follows the pointer lands in day-two operations and finds no policy form. (The Lesson/Module label mix in this file is the Editor's call, not mine; the module number is a factual pointer.)

loc: Lesson04_Maintaining_Veeam_Kasten_Over_Time.html · Upgrades · 02 — Pro tip (keeping pace with Kubernetes)
orig: Put the cluster's Kubernetes upgrade on the same calendar as the Veeam Kasten upgrade, and sequence them deliberately. If the platform team moves the cluster first, your options narrow to whichever Veeam Kasten release supports the new version; if you upgrade Veeam Kasten first, you keep the choice. This is the coordination cost a Veeam Data Platform administrator does not carry when the backup server owns its own Windows host.
prop: Put the cluster's Kubernetes upgrade on the same calendar as the Veeam Kasten upgrade, and sequence them deliberately. Veeam Kasten supports a published list of Kubernetes and OpenShift versions and does not support distribution versions that are no longer actively supported by their vendor or community [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.861, p.862], and a single release can add one version and remove another [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.1098, p.1099] — so if the platform team moves the cluster first, your options narrow to whichever Veeam Kasten release supports the new version, while upgrading Veeam Kasten first keeps the choice. This is the coordination cost a Veeam Data Platform administrator does not carry when the backup server owns its own Windows host.
why: One of the 17 uncited extractions, and the only one carrying operational advice rather than a heading, objective, label or recap. The advice is right and the module has already cited the facts underneath it (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.861, p.862 for the support statement; p.1098, p.1099 for 8.5.9 adding Kubernetes 1.34 and removing 1.30), so grounding it in place costs nothing and makes the sequencing argument checkable by the platform team the admin has to persuade.

loc: Lesson02_Kubernetes_Foundations_for_Backup_Admins.html · Concept · 06 — Prove it before you design around it ("The pre-flight check is a real test")
orig:
The pre-flight check is a real test

The primer tool runs in a pod in the cluster and creates a sample application with a persistent volume, writes data to it, snapshots the volume, creates a new volume from that snapshot, and validates the data in the new volume [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102].
prop:
The CSI pre-flight check is a real test

Run with a specified StorageClass, the primer tool runs in a pod in the cluster and creates a sample application with a persistent volume, writes data to it, snapshots the volume, creates a new volume from that snapshot, and validates the data in the new volume [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]. Lesson 03 covers both invocations: the basic run, and this one.
why: Scope. The end-to-end round trip on Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102 belongs to the CSI pre-flight check deployed 'with a specified StorageClass' ('… | bash /dev/stdin csi -s ${STORAGE_CLASS}'); the plain primer run validates settings, catalogs StorageClasses and does basic CSI validation (Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.7). As written, the foundations lesson tells the learner the default pre-flight already proved the snapshot path — which is exactly the assumption that lets an unverified driver through the readiness gate two lessons later.

loc: Lesson03_Deploying_and_Configuring_Veeam_Kasten.html · Section 3 of 6 · The Helm install — The install command
orig: To use Veeam Kasten with a certified Kubernetes distribution installed on-premises or in another environment you can follow the general instructions, which includes running Veeam Kasten on distributions such as Rancher, PKS, and OKD (OpenShift Origin) [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.99].
prop: To use Veeam Kasten with a certified Kubernetes distribution installed on-premises or in another environment you can follow the general instructions [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.99]. Which distributions those are is a matrix question rather than a name-check: the supported Kubernetes and OpenShift versions are published in the guide, and versions no longer actively supported by their vendor or community are not supported [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.861, p.862].
why: The guide's example list on Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.99 names 'Rancher, PKS, and OKD (OpenShift Origin)' — retired brand names (PKS and the OpenShift Origin name are both several renames behind; that dating is field knowledge, not stated in the 9.0.2 guide, so it is not asserted in the replacement text). Quoting them teaches a learner vocabulary that will make them sound out of date in front of a platform team, and the list adds nothing the sentence needs. Pointing at the supported-version matrix instead is both cited and the answer they actually need before an install.

orig: Veeam Kasten creates Kopia repositories in object store locations, using Kopia as a data mover, which implicitly provides support to deduplicate, encrypt and compress data at rest; Veeam Kasten performs periodic maintenance on these repositories to recover released storage [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315].
prop: Veeam Kasten creates Kopia repositories in object store locations, using Kopia as a data mover, which implicitly provides support to deduplicate, encrypt and compress data at rest — the three things that keep your object storage bill down and your exported data unreadable in transit and at rest, with nothing to configure or remember; Veeam Kasten performs periodic maintenance on these repositories to recover released storage [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.315].
why: Deduplication, encryption, and compression 'at rest, for free' is a real cost and security story a VDP admin would want repeated back to their own leadership, and as written it's filed as trivia in the middle of a paragraph about repository mechanics. Small addition, but it turns a fact dump into a line worth remembering.

Ensure that the csi-snapshotter container for all CSI drivers you might have installed has a minimum version of v1.2.2 — below that, the sidecar is missing capabilities Veeam Kasten depends on to create and clean up snapshots reliably, so this is a check to make before your first policy runs, not a diagnosis to reach for after one fails [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.103].
why: This is an orphaned technical requirement: a version number with zero stated consequence. Everything else in this 'two more storage details that bite later' box explains what breaks if you skip it (the cross-cluster name-matching item does); this one doesn't, so a presenter reading it aloud is just reciting a build number. Low-traffic section of the course, hence minor rather than significant, but worth the one added clause for consistency with its neighbor.

loc: Lesson02_Kubernetes_Foundations_for_Backup_Admins.html · section#namespaces ("Namespaces: where an application lives")
orig: A namespace is a named boundary inside a cluster that holds a set of related objects — workloads, configuration, secrets, storage claims, service definitions. Names are unique within a namespace rather than across the cluster, access control is commonly granted per namespace, and a team is commonly given one to work in. In practice a namespace is how an application is deployed: one namespace, one application, all of its parts inside it.
prop: A namespace is a named boundary inside a cluster that holds a set of related objects — workloads, configuration, secrets, storage claims, service definitions. Names are unique within a namespace rather than across the cluster, access control is commonly granted per namespace, and a team is commonly given one to work in. (On Red Hat OpenShift, which this course also targets, a namespace is wrapped by a Project object that adds default quotas and access policy — the two terms describe the same underlying Kubernetes object [VERIFY: confirm whether Veeam Kasten's own documentation and dashboard use "namespace" or "project" terminology on OpenShift, and note any Project-specific caveat for policy scoping].) In practice a namespace is how an application is deployed: one namespace, one application, all of its parts inside it.
why: The course teaches heavily toward OpenShift (DeploymentConfig, Route, OAuth, OKD) but never once distinguishes "namespace" from OpenShift's Project wrapper — a term an OpenShift-literate reader expects to see addressed the same way the course carefully addresses every other Kubernetes-vs-OpenShift naming nuance. Not a wrong mental model on its own, but a gap in the terminology precision this course otherwise holds itself to.

prop: This walkthrough is abbreviated. The Create Infrastructure Profile wizard has three steps — Name and Provider, Configuration, and Summary — and the two screens below are the two the documentation illustrates [Src: Kasten Docs 9.0.2 p.102]. Treat them as a shape to recognise rather than a complete click path. As with a Location Profile, an Infrastructure Profile is a Kubernetes custom resource under the hood [VERIFY: confirm the CRD name and whether Infrastructure Profiles can be created or edited declaratively the same way Location Profiles can, via the Profiles API] — worth confirming before assuming this step has to stay a dashboard click-path in a GitOps-managed rollout.
why: Section 6 of this same module explicitly tells the reader Location Profiles have a declarative escape hatch ("Location Profile creation can be accessed from the Location page ... or via the CRD-based Profiles API"), but Section 5's Infrastructure Profile walkthrough gives no equivalent pointer — it is presented as dashboard-only. Given how consistently this course otherwise surfaces the CLI/declarative path alongside every GUI walkthrough, this asymmetry reads as an omission rather than a deliberate choice, and it is exactly the kind of gap that makes an expert ask 'where's the YAML' for this one screen.
